Read About Zermatt

A railway village beneath an impossible-looking mountain, shaped as much by restraint as by ambition.

A VILLAGE REMADE BY A MOUNTAIN

Zermatt grew in the upper Matter Valley, where farming settlements lived with long winters and difficult crossings. The Matterhorn was part of that landscape long before it became an international emblem, but the first successful ascent in 1865 transformed the village’s fortunes. Edward Whymper’s party reached the summit, then four climbers died during the descent. Triumph and catastrophe became inseparable parts of Zermatt’s story.

The Matterhorn Museum places that drama inside a wider account of village life. Its reconstructed houses and rooms recall a place of timber, stone and seasonal work, while the broken rope from the 1865 disaster gives the famous ascent a stark physical presence.

Zermatt’s great attraction is not a single viewpoint, but the way the Matterhorn keeps reappearing—above roofs, beyond forests and doubled in still water.

RAILWAYS INTO THE HIGH ALPS

The railway from Visp reached Zermatt in 1891. Seven years later, the Gornergrat Railway began climbing to more than 3,000 metres, making a world of glaciers and four-thousand-metre peaks accessible without mountaineering. The line remains part of the experience: it threads through larch forest before opening onto increasingly broad views of the Monte Rosa massif and the Gorner Glacier.

Another mountain system rises toward Sunnegga and the lakes above it. Leisee, Grindjisee and Stellisee each frame the landscape differently. Their famous reflections depend on calm water and clear skies, which is why an early start matters more than a rigid checklist.

THE CAR-FREE EXPERIMENT

Zermatt chose to limit conventional private cars as tourism expanded. Visitors arrive by rail, while compact electric taxis, hotel shuttles and service vehicles move through the village. The result is quieter than most resorts, though the narrow streets still require attention: the small vehicles approach almost silently.

The old village of Hinterdorf preserves another scale of movement. Larch buildings, some raised on stone discs to deter rodents, stand close together along lanes that predate the resort. Nearby, the Mountaineers’ Cemetery gives names and dates to the risks that built Zermatt’s reputation.

ICE, ALTITUDE AND CHANGE

The cable-car journey to Matterhorn Glacier Paradise ends at 3,883 metres on the Klein Matterhorn. From there, an observation platform looks across an immense borderland of peaks, while the Glacier Palace leads into chambers carved beneath the ice. The experience is engineered, but the cold and thin air are real.

Glacial retreat makes this landscape a record of change as well as a spectacle. The day trip to Brig extends that story at the World Nature Forum, the visitor centre for the Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch UNESCO World Heritage site. It is a useful counterpoint to Zermatt: the Alps appear not only as scenery, but as an inhabited and vulnerable system.
